cvEn:
Giora (Goga) Eitan, son of Rina and Shmuel, was born on the 6th of Tevet 5703 (14 December 1942) in Tel Adashim. He was the third generation of his family in the country. His grandfather was one of the first members of HaShomer and one of the founders of Tel Adashim; his father was a member of the Haganah and one of the founders of the Border Police, and served as a senior officer in the Border Police. His uncle was Brigadier General Raful, the chief paratroop officer.

Giora completed his studies at the Ein Yahav agricultural school. He was interested in sport fishing and pursued it in his leisure time. After completing his compulsory service, he volunteered for the regular army and was promoted to the rank of Captain; he served as a company commander in the Paratroopers. He held the Paratroopers Corps in very high regard, because it was entirely volunteer-based, and he was always ready and prepared to give everything for his homeland. It was the only corps in which he was able to serve, because for him, the path to a combat unit was natural and self-evident, rooted in his home. By home, we do not mean his house in Petah Tikva, to which the family moved when he was twelve, but the home that came before it, Tel Adashim, where he was born and whose atmosphere he longed for in his heart.

From the agricultural school where he studied, he joined the Nahal garin (pioneer group) and was among the founders of kibbutz Ein Yahav in the Arava. There too his pioneering spirit was evident, and from his kibbutz he went on to become a paratrooper, serving in Nahal Paratroopers.

When the Six-Day War broke out, Giora went to the front. In the battle for the Sheikh Zuweid positions in Sinai, on the first day of fighting, the 26th of Iyar 5727 (5 June 1967), his armored personnel carrier was hit by a shell. Although he was seriously wounded, he continued to command his comrades and men to the end, for as long as he remained conscious.

He left behind a wife and a daughter (just over two years old). His son, born in August 1967, about two months after his father fell, was named after him. He was buried in the emergency military cemetery at Beeri, and later reinterred in the cemetery in Petah Tikva. A cover story about him was published in *BaMahane* under the title "The World of Paratroop Officer Giora Eitan."
